articles.title: Iranian lawmaker says Tehran would respond in kind if US used nuclear weapon
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026
An Iranian lawmaker said Tehran would respond in kind if the US used a nuclear weapon against Iran, commenting on a media report about the possibility of such an attack, according to local media on Wednesday.
Fada Hossein Maleki, a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, made the remarks in an interview with Iranian news outlet Khabar Online.
Asked how likely he considered a US nuclear attack on Iran, Maleki said: “I do not rule out an ill-considered action by (US President Donald) Trump, but I do not think he would dare to do such a thing, because such an action could plunge the world into a dangerous war.”
“If such an action is taken, the Islamic Republic of Iran will also respond, and its reaction will be proportionate to the type of weapon used against Iran,” he added.
Pressed on whether this meant Iran would use a nuclear weapon if the US attacked Iran with one, Maleki replied: “Whatever the US uses, Iran will respond to it.”
Maleki did not explicitly say that Iran possesses nuclear weapons.
The lawmaker also warned Washington against further military action, saying Iran has “multiple options” at its disposal and that any US move could draw a response “at the same level or even beyond.”
“Many of Iran’s weapons and military capabilities have not yet been unveiled,” Maleki said, arguing that Tehran has moved from a defensive posture to what he described as “active and offensive deterrence.”
Turning to stalled Tehran-Washington talks, Maleki accused Trump of failing to honor commitments under the memorandum of understanding between the two sides.
He said Iran would not return to negotiations unless Washington abides by its previous commitments, adding that issues including the Strait of Hormuz would remain unresolved otherwise.
Maleki said Iran’s talks with Oman are a separate bilateral track, adding that Tehran rejected US participation in those discussions.
Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June under Pakistani mediation aimed at ending their war and paving the way for negotiations on a final agreement.
Talks have since stalled amid disputes over the implementation of the memorandum, including issues related to the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest tensions follow months of hostilities since the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate against US and Israeli targets and US assets across the region.

articles.title: In cutting joint drills, Trump has given South Korea’s president what he wants. So why is Seoul so uneasy?
articles.body:
At their first summit, in August last year, the South Korean president, Lee Jae Myung, told Donald Trump: “If you, Mr President, become the peacemaker, then I will assist you as the pacemaker.”
The remark at the Oval Office captured the thrust of Lee’s approach to North Korea: dial down the military posturing and make repeated peace overtures to revive dialogue, even if they have been consistently rejected by Pyongyang largely over Seoul’s insistence on denuclearisation.
Fast forward to this week, and Trump’s move to cut joint military exercises with South Korea echoes what Lee had himself floated, on several occasions, as a possible tool for drawing Pyongyang back to the table.
Lee’s broader message is that South Korea should take more responsibility for its own defence and reduce its reliance on others. On Tuesday, he used the moment to renew calls for wartime operational control of the military and progress on his country’s nuclear submarine programme.
Trump has delivered on the drills, albeit in the blunt, discourteous fashion typical of the president: via social media, hours before the drills were to begin.
Yet the move has inverted South Korea’s usual political lines, where the left-right divide is shaped more by attitudes toward North Korea – hawks v doves, confrontation v engagement – than by economic or social values.
Reducing joint drills has long been advocated by some on the Korean left. A rightwing US president imposing the policy on his centre-left South Korean counterpart lands awkwardly for both sides.
While some see the reduction as potentially useful for diplomacy, the louder concern in Seoul is that Trump is weakening a key pillar of deterrence, and leaving South Korea with little say over decisions that directly affect its security. That may strain an alliance that has been the bedrock of security on the peninsula since the Korean war.
The opposition conservative People Power party has called the decision a “security disaster” and warned of a return to “Korea passing”, a term used when Seoul feels sidelined in matters directly affecting it. Conservative newspapers have been almost unanimous in calling the cut reckless. The influential Chosun Ilbo has gone further, blaming Lee’s government directly for inviting it.
The left has not shared that sense of alarm. Hankyoreh, one of the country’s main progressive papers, raised no objection to the substance of Trump’s decision, only to how it was delivered: unilaterally and disrespectfully on social media, calling it “regrettable”. Kyunghyang Shinmun took a more positive view, saying the cut could help create an atmosphere for dialogue with North Korea, so long as deterrence held.
Reducing tensions with North Korea and creating space for dialogue are central to Lee’s agenda. The ruling party has been quiet on the move, but openly welcoming Trump’s decision could put it at odds with a base that has generally viewed Trump with suspicion, if not hostility.
Aside from the domestic politics, the episode is likely to deepen doubts about Washington’s commitment to its allies, doubts that have been building for years since Trump’s first term, said Prof Jaechun Kim, who teaches international relations at Sogang University, in Seoul.
Trust, he argued, is the foundation of any alliance, and remarks like Trump’s reinforce the impression that the US’s obligations are increasingly viewed “through a highly transactional lens”, one that could shape how South Koreans judge US reliability long after Trump has left office.
Then there is the issue of the nuclear deterrent. South Korea enjoys protection under the US nuclear umbrella, but public support for an independent deterrent among South Koreans and their neighbours has hovered around or above 70% in recent surveys. The latest news may push that support higher still.
Kim said he expects Pyongyang to welcome any sign of friction within the alliance but doubts that it views improving relations with Washington as a priority, given the stronger backing it now enjoys from China and Russia compared with during Trump’s first term.
“The irony,” he said, “is that [US] policies intended to reduce American burdens may ultimately strengthen calls for independent nuclear deterrents among US allies.”

articles.title: Iran's parliament speaker Ghalibaf begins two-day Baghdad visit
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iranian parliament speaker Ghalibaf begins Baghdad visit, set to meet Coordination Framework
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf began a two-day official visit to Iraq on Wednesday morning, 19 August, amid mounting US pressure on Iran-aligned Popular Mobilisation factions, regional tensions and strained relations between Iran and Arab neighbouring countries.
Upon arriving at Baghdad International Airport, Ghalibaf immediately headed to the site where former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani was assassinated.
Soleimani was killed in a US airstrike in 2020 shortly after arriving in Baghdad from Damascus, alongside Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis.
From there, Ghalibaf said, "Our visit comes to discuss cooperation between the countries of the region without foreign interference. The Islamic countries in the region need to expand areas of cooperation and establish deep and sustainable relations", he said. "Iran is making efforts in this regard."
During his visit to Iraq, he will meet several senior government officials, a statement added.
Ghalibaf to attend Coordination Framework meeting
According to a source in the Iraqi Foreign Ministry who spoke to The New Arab, Ghalibaf will attend a scheduled meeting of Iraq's ruling coalition, the Coordination Framework, on Wednesday in the presence of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.
The source described the meeting as "closed", noting that the Iranian official wants to present Iran's position on the US presence in Iraq and the issue of placing weapons held by the state and factions under state control.
The deadline for resolving the issue expires on 30 September.
Before heading to Baghdad, Ghalibaf said in an Arabic-language post on X that "the relationship between the Iranian and Iraqi peoples is a historic and inseparable one.
"Our neighbourhood was built based on brotherhood during the most difficult days, resistance to foreign interference, and belief in the shared destiny of both countries. This rich past, full of lessons, will be a beacon for the future," he wrote.
The Iranian parliament speaker added, "During this visit, we will take practical and major steps to consolidate self-reliant and shared security for both countries and achieve prosperity for both peoples."
"Our brothers are our strength," he concluded.
Visit programme
In this context, the Iranian ambassador to Iraq, Mohammad Kazem Al-e Sadeq, told Iranian news agency ISNA that Ghalibaf will meet during his visit with the speaker of parliament, the prime minister, the president, the president of the Supreme Judicial Council and the national security adviser in Iraq.
They will hold talks on bilateral, regional and international issues.
Al-e Sadeq added that the meetings would include an exchange of views on bilateral, regional and international issues, stressing that the visit is of "great importance" amid developments in the region.
He said consultations between the two countries could help strengthen regional stability and calm.
The Iranian ambassador stressed that the visit had been scheduled in advance and came in response to an official invitation from Iraqi Parliament Speaker Haibat al-Halbousi.
Asked whether Ghalibaf's visit was linked to recent developments in relations between the two countries, and notably, the targeting of Iraqi Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, Al-e Sadeq denied any connection, saying, "There is no connection, and this visit, as I mentioned earlier, had been scheduled in advance."
He noted that the Iranian parliament speaker will participate on Thursday, 20 August, in the Arbaeen ceremony marking the burial of the late Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, to be held in Karbala.
The Kurdistan Region's Counter-Terrorism Service announced on Monday, 17 August, that Barzani's office in Erbil had been targeted by an Iranian drone, as well as the home of the head of the security and intelligence service.
However, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei implicitly denied his country's involvement in the attack on Monday evening by condemning it.
He described it as a "highly suspicious development" and called for the incident to be handled "with vigilance and precision".

articles.title: US targets ICC chief in push to ‘dismantle’ court
articles.body:
US targets ICC chief in push to ‘dismantle’ court
The US has imposed sanctions on two senior International Criminal Court (ICC) officials, accusing The Hague-based institution of overstepping its authority.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday designated ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye, describing the court as a “corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate.”
The designations are a part of a campaign announced by Rubio last month to “systematically dismantle the threat posed” by the ICC to US sovereignty.
Rubio has accused the court of targeting nationals of countries that have neither consented to its jurisdiction nor ratified the Rome Statute. The ICC previously investigated alleged crimes by US military and intelligence personnel in Afghanistan despite Washington not being a member.
Israel likewise rejects the court’s jurisdiction. Nevertheless, in 2024 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. A February 2025 executive order signed by US President Donald Trump condemned the warrants.
Seye worked on the prosecution team involved in the Netanyahu case. Israeli outlet Ynet reported in May that he was also overseeing an ICC investigation into funding for West Bank settlements and the supply of weapons to settlers. Netanyahu welcomed the latest US sanctions, denouncing the ICC as a “kangaroo court.”
The ICC said on Wednesday it “strongly rejects” the new designations, calling them “a flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution.”
The court has also faced criticism elsewhere. Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger have initiated withdrawals this summer, while Chad followed in July, accusing the ICC of disproportionately focusing on Africa.
The Philippines withdrew in 2019, but the ICC maintained jurisdiction over crimes allegedly committed while the country was a member. Former President Rodrigo Duterte was arrested under an ICC warrant in March 2025 over alleged crimes against humanity linked to killings during his anti-drug campaign and transferred to The Hague.
Russia has likewise rejected the court’s authority. The ICC issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in March 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia. Moscow dismissed the warrants as legally null and void and rejected the allegations, saying it evacuated unaccompanied children from the war zone and is ready to return them to their legal guardians upon request.

articles.title: Longtime publisher of Stars and Stripes to retire, citing differences with Pentagon leadership
articles.body:
Longtime publisher of Stars and Stripes to retire, citing differences with Pentagon leadership
The longtime publisher of Stars and Stripes has announced his retirement, ending a decades-long career with the military newspaper as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon moves to exert editorial control and eliminate what it asserts are “woke distractions.”
Max D. Lederer Jr. announced his retirement, effective at the end of September, in a memo to staff on Tuesday, as well as in an interview with Stars and Stripes. In the memo, seen by The Associated Press, Lederer, the second full-time civilian in the position, wrote that it had “become clear that my philosophy of leadership, and my understanding of the value and mission of Stars and Stripes, differ in fundamental ways from the direction the leadership of the Department of Defense has for the organization.”
The announcement comes less than four months after the Pentagon fired Jacqueline Smith, ombudsman for the newspaper, whose job was to safeguard editorial independence. The news outlet is partly funded by the Defense Department, but has a legacy of independence from military and government leadership. “No one should be surprised that they’re kicking out the one person charged by Congress with protecting Stars and Stripes’ editorial independence,” Smith wrote in a column.
Stars and Stripes has recently been at the forefront of some of the reporting on conditions for sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln and concerns for their mental health during the aircraft carrier’s long deployment — concerns that President Donald Trump has downplayed.
It’s part of larger, government-driven changes to the military publication
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lederer’s retirement, which comes seven months after the department announced in a social media post that it would essentially overhaul the newspaper to align with its current messaging.
Hegseth’s spokesman, Sean Parnell, wrote on on X in January that the Pentagon “is returning Stars and Stripes to its original mission: reporting for our warfighters.” He said the department will “refocus its content away from woke distractions.”
“Stars and Stripes will be custom tailored to our warfighters,” Parnell wrote. “It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability and ALL THINGS MILITARY. No more repurposed DC gossip columns; no more Associated Press reprints.”
More broadly, the developments at Stars and Stripes come against a backdrop of increased efforts by Hegseth to control media coverage of the department.
Last year, officials attempted to impose restrictions on journalists working inside the Pentagon, which, in turn, led most news outlets to turn in their access badges and walk out.
Then this summer, the Pentagon took another step and declared its press office a classified space — instituting a policy that journalists must be accompanied by an escort on Pentagon grounds. That policy is being challenged in court. In mid-July, a panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit said the policy could stand, overturning a lower court decision.
In her April column titled “The Pentagon is trying to silence me,” Smith, the former ombudsman, expressed concern over increasing restrictions on the media.
“For nearly a year, Pentagon leadership has placed more and more restrictions on the mainstream media,” she wrote. “The New York Times sued and when the Defense/War Department lost in court, instead of following the judge’s ruling Secretary Hegseth and company pivoted, finding another way to restrict journalists.”
Of Stars and Stripes, Smith wrote: “This newspaper has a long history of commitment to the military community and to journalistic values. Please don’t let it be controlled by Pentagon brass.”
The departing publisher objected to certain changes
Lederer was not made available for an interview with the AP. In the interview with Stars and Stripes, he said he did not feel the modernization efforts the Pentagon announced in March were appropriate, in particular a transitioning of print products to digital — a move he feared would limit accessibility for troops.
“I don’t feel that there’s a full recognition of the value of multiple platforms versus only a digital platform,” Lederer was quoted as saying.
In another development, Stars and Stripes said it could not confirm an account that, in recent weeks, a new deputy had been installed by the Pentagon under Lederer without the publisher’s prior knowledge.
In a letter seen by the AP, Rufus Friday, the chair of Stars and Stripes’ advisory board of publishers, wrote to congressional leaders about the arrival of the new deputy, a development he said “threatens Stripes’s editorial independence.”
Roughly half of Stars and Stripes’ budget comes from the Pentagon, and its staff members are considered Defense Department employees.
The outlet’s mission statement emphasizes that it is “editorially independent of interference from outside its own editorial chain-of-command” and that it is unique among news organizations tied to the Defense Department in being “governed by the principles of the First Amendment.”
The newspaper has been reporting about the military steadily since World War II, to an audience mainly of service members stationed overseas.
Lederer told Stars and Stripes that while his retirement is effective Sept. 30, he does not know whether the Pentagon will keep him as publisher until then or name an acting publisher.
___
Jocelyn Noveck writes about the intersection of media and entertainment for the AP.

articles.title: Ye (Kanye West) sold 100,000 tickets to two St. Petersburg stadium shows in two days. Now a Russian lawmaker wants the concerts canceled unless he declares ‘moral support’ for the war on Ukraine.
articles.body:
Ye (Kanye West) sold 100,000 tickets to two St. Petersburg stadium shows in two days. Now a Russian lawmaker wants the concerts canceled unless he declares ‘moral support’ for the war on Ukraine.
On October 10 and 11, American rapper Ye (Kanye West) will perform at Gazprom Arena in St. Petersburg. Organizers say they have sold more than 100,000 tickets in the first two days. And the hype shows no sign of fading: lawmakers in the State Duma (Russia’s lower house of parliament), public figures, and, of course, social media users are all discussing Ye’s visit. Meduza rounded up the biggest news, rumors, and memes about the rapper’s concerts in Russia.
Earlier this week, State Duma deputy Vitaly Milonov suggested that Ye add Russian chanson — a genre of sentimental ballads steeped in prison folklore — to his repertoire. Milonov said the rapper could perform songs by Mikhail Krug or sing a duet with Mikhail Shufutinsky while in St. Petersburg. Such a move, Milonov said, would help Ye become a “normal person.”
The saga then took a turn: on August 18, reports began circulating on social media that the rapper wanted to perform with Shaman, the pro-war Russian singer. Concert organizers had supposedly approached the singer’s booking manager with the request, and, judging by a screenshot of the exchange, Shaman turned it down. The organizers, for their part, denied that any such talks took place
Social media users think the duet could be a hit, hinting that Ye — who has publicly professed admiration for Hitler and the Nazis — has plenty in common with Shaman.
Sergei Shnurov, the frontman of the band Leningrad, has also angled for a chance to perform with Ye. But so far, no invitation has come.
Other collaboration ideas are floating around, too. The promotional blitz for the film The Last Warrior. Kolobok has been hard to miss in Russia. And social media users have a suggestion to boost its box-office performance.
Others suggest branding the entire stage — or at least adding a bit of local flavor. Russian authorities, though, appear to have their own plans for the venue.
Either way, the priority is avoiding another round of internet outages — and the American performer had better not turn on a VPN either, just in case.
Lawmakers in the State Duma have yet to make up their minds about the controversial performer’s visit. Yelena Drapeko of A Just Russia, for one, believes the concerts should go ahead, and even publicly thanked the rapper for agreeing to come “amid anti-Russian hysteria.” Svetlana Zhurova of United Russia has gone further, floating the idea of a meeting between Ye and Russian President Vladimir Putin — though Ye would first have to take a COVID-19 test.
Anna Subcheva, who heads Say Agency, the company organizing the event, said meeting Putin has long been Ye’s dream. She said Ye has voiced admiration for the Russian president “for several years now.” What the rapper actually dreams of is anyone’s guess, but he did once call himself a “young Putin.”
Nikolai Novichkov of A Just Russia said earlier that he would push to cancel the concerts if Ye failed to declare “moral support” for the SVO — the Kremlin’s shorthand for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which it calls a ”special military operation.” Ildar Rezyapov, head of the Veterans of Russia movement, called for part of the concert proceeds to go to Russian troops. Yekaterina Mizulina, head of the Safe Internet League, and several Orthodox priests have also objected to the visit.
Social media users are joking that the authorities themselves don’t fully grasp whom they’ve invited to Russia. They’re also offering some distinctly peculiar ways to “support the war.”
Meanwhile, the rapper’s Russian fans are already imagining how they’ll welcome him. A guest like this, they joke, calls for the good china — and a city scrubbed clean for the occasion.
Others propose renaming the Leningrad region outright in recognition of Ye’s talent.
Ye’s visit has even shaken up the rental housing market. The Russian business outlet RBC reported that demand for short-term rentals has risen at least sevenfold — or 16-fold, by other estimates. Demand for train tickets on the concert dates has jumped 41-fold. One thing worth remembering: a 160,000-ruble ticket in the VIP boxes buys one seat, not the whole box for a group of friends.

articles.title: Ukraine’s 25th Airborne Brigade moves ground robots from testing to combat
articles.body:
In an interview with Army Inform, Colonel Illia Petryna, commander of the 25th Separate Sicheslav Airborne Brigade, said the brigade created a ground-robotics company as a pilot unit and that it was among the first Ukrainian brigades to organize ground robots this way.
The company was initially created to test how the systems could work in combat. They are now being used for different battlefield tasks, Petryna said. Some robots carry supplies. Others are used for evacuation or provide fire support.
The move is part of Ukraine's broader effort to build dedicated units around ground robots. In February 2025, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said the military was forming units focused on unmanned ground systems after testing that had begun in summer 2024. The systems were already being used for logistics, fire strikes, and evacuating wounded soldiers.
Ukraine has since continued expanding their use. By March 2026, 167 units were using ground robots, up from 67 in November 2025. More than 9,000 combat and logistical missions were conducted with unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) that month, according to the Defense Ministry.
Learning from the battlefield
The 25th's robotic company also gives soldiers a way to test systems and report problems directly to manufacturers.
“Cooperation with manufacturers is the basis,” Petryna said. “They draw information from us about what is needed now, what is relevant at the front.”
Soldiers use the machines in combat, identify what does not work, and pass that information back to manufacturers. The next versions can then be adapted to conditions at the front.
That creates a direct feedback loop between the battlefield and the companies developing the technology.
Petryna sees that constant adaptation as necessary because the technology and tactics of the war keep changing.
“Probably, right now, no statute in the world fits how this war is being fought,” he said. “The war has changed fundamentally.”
For the 25th, the robotic company is one way to keep adapting as the battlefield changes.

articles.title: Ukraine’s new defense minister says he already knows Russia’s strategy for fall and winter
articles.body:
Yevhenii Khmara has become Ukraine's new defense minister after the voting in the Ukrainian parliament. He will take office after the previous Minister of Defense, Mykhailo Fedorov, whose dismissal sparked major protests across Ukraine, but this did not change the decision.
During his first speech, Khmara made it clear that he would continue his predecessor's course — the technologization of the army, according to Ukraine's Defense Ministry.
"The aggressor can only be forced into peace through the strength of our military, technological, and asymmetric solutions, first and foremost, the constant updating and effective application of technology," Khmara said.
He added that there "would be more Ukrainian weapons, and strikes would be more precise."
Threat of new wave of mobilization in Russia
Khmara also stated that intelligence data indicates Russia is preparing for a new wave of mobilization, so building up the means to destroy Russia's combat capabilities is one of the key priorities of the Defense Forces.
"A strong enemy is waging war against us, one that employs the most treacherous and cruel methods of warfare. We know about Russia's next steps, its mobilization plans, and its strategy for fall and winter," Khmara stated.
Earlier, Deputy Head of the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence, Major General Vadym Skibitsky, said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine that Russia could attempt to launch an offensive in north of Ukraine this year, but the necessary conditions for such an operation are not currently in place. Such an assault could threat Sumy, Chernihiv, and Kyiv oblasts.
Opportunities for this could arise through mobilization following the parliamentary elections in the Russian Federation in September.
Three main priorities
Also, during his speech, Khmara outlined three priorities for his position. Among them: seizing the strategic initiative in all domains of war, timely delivery of weapons to the front along with transparent procurement procedures, and human capital.
"This is about seizing the strategic initiative in all domains of war: on land, at sea, in the air, in the information space," Khmara stated.
He also emphasized the need to ensure rapid exchange of information between the front and the ministry, so that the needs of the military are promptly taken into account when making decisions.
According to the newly appointed minister, the army must receive the necessary weapons in sufficient quantities and on time, and procurement must be carried out transparently, free of unnecessary bureaucracy, and in the interests of the front and Ukraine's defense.
In addition, Khmara named "human capital, the lives and health of soldiers" as a priority.
"Technology is needed so that the Ukrainian defender has an advantage, so that the risk to a person's life is minimized," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine's military intelligence publishes data on six Russian propagandists
articles.body:
Ukraine's military intelligence publishes data on six Russian propagandists
Ukrinform
    The Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) and the Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD) at the National Security and Defense Council have published information on six Russian public figures who support Russia's armed aggression and are directly involved in the Kremlin's information war against Ukraine.
    HUR reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
The information was published in the "Kremlin Mouthpieces" section of the War&Sanctions portal. They include:
- Sergey Tovkach – a Russian developer of unmanned systems and author of the Telegram channel "UAV Developer." He spreads anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, publishes material from combat zones, organizes fundraising campaigns to support participants in Russia's so-called "special military operation," and shares technical information and advice on the use of UAVs by Russian armed forces against Ukraine.
- Alexey Chadayev – a Russian publicist and political strategist, adviser to Russia's transport minister and CEO of the Ushkuynik National Project Center. He is one of the organizers of technological support for Russia's aggression against Ukraine in the field of unmanned aerial systems.
- Roman Golovanov – a correspondent for the domestic politics section of the Komsomolskaya Pravda publishing house and a host on the Spas and Soloviev Live television channels. He spreads disinformation and destructive narratives, including false claims about alleged "persecution of the Orthodox Church and Christianity" in Ukraine.
The "Kremlin Mouthpieces" section of the War&Sanctions portal already contains information on nearly 200 Russian propaganda figures who justify Russia's aggression and war crimes, manipulate socially significant information, spread disinformation about developments on the battlefield, and seek to influence public opinion in various regions of the world.
HUR and CCD called on partner countries to impose individual sanctions on members of Russia's propaganda apparatus, restrict their entry, freeze their financial assets, and terminate media and commercial cooperation with them.

articles.title: Israel's Syria strike risked scrambling Turkish jets, military escalation, US envoy tells 'Post'
articles.body:
On Tuesday evening, the Prime Minister’s Office took credit for a strike on Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib, Syria. US ambassador to Turkey and the Trump administration’s special envoy to Syria, Tom Barrack, said that the strike “carried a real risk of rapid escalation into a direct military confrontation between Israel and Turkey as well as Syria.”
“Turkish forces were not aware that the Israeli aircraft were en route to that specific Syrian base, nor of their intended purpose, and therefore could potentially have been inclined to scramble their own jets in the belief that they themselves were under attack,” Barrack said in a Wednesday interview with The Jerusalem Post.
“The events of yesterday were serious and worrisome. However, we are relieved that no human life was harmed and that the situation did not escalate,” he added.
Syria said on Tuesday that Israel had carried out eight airstrikes on the runway and storage facilities at Abu al-Duhur, about 70 kilometers east of the Turkish border.
The Prime Minister’s Office said late Tuesday that Syria was on the “verge” of violating a “status quo agreed with Israel on security matters” by allowing Turkish troops to deploy at the airbase.
“Israel repeatedly warned Syria that such a deployment would pose a threat to Israel’s security. Syria chose to ignore these warnings,” the PMO said.
Barrack told the Post that the lack of clear communication channels could have made the situation “much worse,” and that this needs to change.
Barrack: Discussions ongoing about relaunching Israel-Syria deconfliction cell
“We are currently engaged in quiet discussions with all the relevant parties about relaunching a deconfliction cell between Israel and Syria. Turkey can be invited to be a direct or indirect participant,” Barrack said.
“There would be clear value in placing such an arrangement on a standing, full-time basis, with a fusion cell staffed around the clock by personnel fluent in Hebrew, Arabic, English, and Turkish, whether through a formal structure or a more flexible, informal channel. Reliable communication remains essential,” he added.
The Trump envoy said that the absence of dependable communication channels itself creates unnecessary risk.
“There is no inherent obstacle preventing these parties from maintaining open lines of communication. Diplomatic discourse is the best prevention to kinetic interactions,” he said.
IN RECENT years, Barrack has hosted several rounds of discussions between Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government and senior Israeli officials in an attempt to reach a border agreement between the countries, advance normalization, and de-escalate tensions.
“Meaningful progress was achieved in clarifying the concerns of both parties, and in light of recent developments, there is clear value in revisiting these talks at the earliest opportunity,” Barrack told the Post, adding that the Sharaa government has made clear that it harbors no predatory intentions toward Israel and seeks only to protect its own sovereignty.
“Syria has demonstrated itself to be a responsible and stable sovereign neighbor, and a carefully structured de-escalation arrangement would contribute significantly to greater calm and predictability across the region,” Barrack said.
Israeli concerns over Turkish military equipment close to Syria-Israeli border remains sticking point
One of the sticking points during the talks was Israel’s concern that Turkish military personnel or equipment could be deployed at Syrian bases, some of them close to the Israeli border.
In January, the Post reported that the deployment of an advanced Turkish HTRS-100 radar system at Damascus International Airport was viewed in Israel as “extremely troubling.”
Israeli officials feared that a Turkish military installation capable of tracking aerial targets within a 150-200 kilometer range could significantly restrict the Israel Air Force’s freedom of movement in Syrian airspace.
Barrack said that, in the US view, the civilian infrastructure does not pose a security threat to Israel.
“Syria’s ability to maintain safe and reliable domestic aviation depends on functioning civilian radar coverage. We remain convinced that this technical requirement need not pose a security concern, and that further conversations can help clarify the matter to everyone’s satisfaction,” he told the Post.
Barrack added that the US’s immediate priority must be to help lower tensions between Ankara and Jerusalem and prevent any unintended escalation that could prove difficult to reverse.
“All parties should work patiently toward a durable resolution of this highly complex situation. Turkey and Israel have, at various points over the past three decades, enjoyed periods of constructive and productive relations. President [Donald] Trump’s plan offers a viable path that can succeed if given the necessary space and support,” he said.

articles.title: Russians recruited for war in Ukraine through jobs as guards at Wildberries and Ozon warehouses, Verstka reports
articles.body:
About 2,000 ads seeking guards for “mobile fire groups” at warehouses run by Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon have appeared on the online classifieds site Avito since Aug. 17, the exiled independent Russian outlet Verstka reported today. Recruiters are offering candidates a one-year contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry, claiming that those who sign up will not be sent to fight in Ukraine. However, sources interviewed by the outlet said the vacancies are a cover for ordinary recruitment of contract soldiers.
Almost all of the ads bear the same headline: “Security for Wildberries and Ozon warehouses as part of a [mobile fire] group.” The ads urge applicants to sign a contract before the start of “mobilization processes,” promising a one-time up-front bonus of 3.1 million rubles ($37,000). The application deadline listed in the ads was Aug. 15 — two days before they actually appeared en masse.
A Verstka correspondent, posing as a job seeker, called the phone numbers listed in two of the ads. Recruiters said candidates would sign a one-year “special contract” with Russia's Ministry of Defense, then get to work defending commercial warehouses from drones. One recruiter said Wildberries itself had allegedly asked the ministry to arrange such security measures.
The recruiters assured the journalist that those who signed the contract would not be sent to the front lines in Ukraine. Nevertheless, the registration procedure does not differ from ordinary recruitment for the invasion: candidates are asked to hand over their documents, sign a contract with the Defense Ministry, and undergo training in Tula. One recruiter warned that without an application filed through him, the applicant would be sent by the enlistment office directly to the combat zone.
The phone numbers to which the correspondent was told to send documents were labeled in caller ID apps as “Olesya SVO” and “Central Military District enlistment office.”
Three Verstka sources connected to military recruitment efforts said the ads were a cover for recruiting contract soldiers. Two of the sources said recruiters disguise military service offers as civilian jobs because Avito strictly moderates such posts.
Media outlets have previously found hidden online offers for military service disguised as jobs for drivers of humanitarian cargo, guards at warehouses in Belarus, and vaguely defined “peacekeepers.” The new ads appeared amid a series of drone attacks on Wildberries logistics centers.

articles.title: A Ukrainian army medic was captured by Russian troops, raped in custody, and put on trial for terrorism. Her sons ended up on opposite sides of the war. Here’s what happened to her family.
articles.body:
A Ukrainian army medic was captured by Russian troops, raped in custody, and put on trial for terrorism. Her sons ended up on opposite sides of the war. Here’s what happened to her family.
Liliia Prutian is a Ukrainian from the Donbas, a former military medic with the Aidar Battalion, and a mother of three sons. After the full-scale invasion began, she endured rape and captivity. Her oldest son served in Ukraine’s armed forces, her middle son joined the Russian army, and her youngest was stranded in occupied territory as a teenager and spent three years surviving there on his own. The New York Times told the family’s story, speaking to Prutian and two of her sons. Meduza summarizes that report.
Prutian, 56, is a widow with three sons from the village of Blyzhnie in Ukraine’s Donetsk region. She worked at a gas station for $140 a month until 2017, when she took a job with the Ukrainian army that paid two and a half times as much. She served first as an accountant, later as a military medic.
Prutian wound up in the Aidar Battalion, which, along with Azov, became a symbol of “Ukrainian Nazism” in Russian propaganda after 2014. The posting took her far from home. Her two older sons were already adults. Dima, the youngest, was just 12.
Prutian came home every two or three weeks. While she was away, Dima’s brothers and other relatives looked after him. She told herself it was the only way to support her family. She also felt the army had given her a sense of purpose, The New York Times wrote.
After February 24, 2022, Aidar was sent to the Mariupol area. Sixteen days into the full-scale invasion, Russian troops surrounded Prutian and several of her fellow soldiers. A Russian soldier raped her in captivity. Her captors initially planned to gang-rape her, Prutian said, but, sobbing, she asked them, “Please let it be just one of you.” “You could say they met me halfway,” she later told The New Yorker.
What followed was a cell in Donetsk, then one in Rostov. The toilet stopped working, so Prutian and her cellmates saved leftover soup and used the broth to flush it. Then came a trial on terrorism charges. Then, before any verdict, she was suddenly released in a prisoner swap. Once she was back on Ukrainian-held soil, her greatest worry was Dima.
Russian forces occupied Blyzhnie, the family’s hometown, in the first month of the full-scale invasion. Dima, then 17, was left alone in the house. His mother wrote and called when she could, and then the messages stopped. His oldest brother, like her, was serving in the Ukrainian army, far from home. His middle brother lived on his own and did not share the rest of the family’s pro-Ukrainian views.
Dima had been studying at a forestry college before the full-scale war began. Now his classes had stopped, and there were no jobs. He asked his oldest brother, who was fighting for Ukraine, to keep sending him money for groceries. In September 2022, complications from his Type 1 diabetes left him seriously ill. His middle brother drove him to the hospital and left him there, never once visiting. He stayed for months, until a teacher from his school found him and signed him out.
It was around then, Prutian said, that her middle son chose sides for good. He married a pro-Russian Ukrainian woman, sold his mother’s car, stopped speaking to his brothers and soon enlisted in the Russian army. Later, during her terrorism trial in Russia, her middle son’s written testimony against her was read out — that was how she learned he had joined the Russian army.
When he got back from the hospital in the winter of 2023, Dima found Russian soldiers in his house. The soldiers soon moved out, taking with them a laptop, cutlery, Prutian’s jewelry, and even some of Dima’s clothes and shoes. He went back to school, took a part-time construction job, and got a Russian passport, which he needed to keep studying, pay his utilities, and collect aid rations.
After her release, Prutian ended up at a rehabilitation center on the outskirts of Kyiv. There she underwent surgery to restore hearing she had lost after her ears were damaged in combat, and worked out how to get back Dima. She feared that if he stayed in Blyzhnie, he would eventually be forced into the Russian army. When they finally managed to make contact, Dima confirmed he wanted to leave.
To get her youngest son out, Prutian paid a taxi driver about $115 to smuggle him a temporary Ukrainian passport and hired another to drive him out of occupied territory. The only practical way out led through Russia, and from there he continued on to Belarus and Poland, covering 1,740 miles before meeting his mother in Kyiv. He ran to her and hugged her tightly, but Prutian felt oddly numb. “I can’t say I felt joy. Meeting him felt like meeting a stranger. They say that’s normal after captivity,” she told The New York Times.
Dima reached his mother in late February 2025, three years after the full-scale invasion began. At first he was so withdrawn that he asked permission for everything and barely spoke, but in time they adjusted to living together again. Prutian and Dima now live in Dnipro. She still works for the Ukrainian army, now at a desk job far from the front. He has resumed his studies. Prutian’s oldest son, now discharged from the Ukrainian military, lives with them. People back home told her that her middle son had suffered a head wound in a drone attack. She did not try to find out more.

articles.title: Many Russians who left because of the war had to start over abroad. Some found careers they never expected.
articles.body:
Many Russians who left because of the war had to start over abroad. Some found careers they never expected.
People who left Russia after the start of the full-scale war have had to start their lives over from scratch. They’ve had to learn a new language, absorb the local culture, traditions, and bureaucracy, adjust to the climate, and make new friends and acquaintances. Many lost their jobs during the move or after arriving in a new country and were forced — despite having a college degree and a strong portfolio — to take low-paying jobs. But some have learned new professions in emigration and are happy with them. Meduza tells the difficult, but in some ways even inspiring, stories of these Russians.
Ksenia Borovinskaya, 37
From a copywriter in Moscow to a bar founder in Buenos Aires
Before I emigrated, I was never idle — I was always finding good freelance work through people I knew. I wrote copy for Afisha Daily and Mel, and for shampoo and wet-wipe packaging. In 2018, an acquaintance helped me land a job at RusTransplant, a project for organ transplant patients, where I wrote guides on eating right, exercising, and having sex safely after a transplant.
The Moscow Health Ministry funded the project. In the war’s first few days, our director told us the ministry had set a condition for continued funding: staff members and the project itself had to publicly support the war on social media. Everyone refused.
I left Russia in March 2022 with my two young children and our dog. It was hard on the kids, but they understood why we left. In the war’s first days, my older son drew a tank with a line through it at school; his teacher handed me the drawing and asked that he not do it again. We wouldn’t have been allowed to live in peace in Russia.
We flew to Armenia first. Armenian turned out to be so difficult that in two months I learned only a few letters. I hadn’t expected Armenia to be so cold, and I was a wreck, unable to pull myself together.
At some point, a friend called from Argentina and said, “Come here: there’s no war, and people drink wine.” I thought Argentina might help me reset and recover, so I decided to move. Just before that, I learned I’d been fired from RusTransplant for working remotely. I used my last paycheck to buy tickets to Buenos Aires.
In Argentina, I applied for political asylum, citing my antiwar stance and the risk of persecution in Russia — police, for one, had already come looking for me at my registered address. I was issued a temporary residency certificate that let me live and work in the country legally.
I got my first job in Argentina out of pity, a month after I arrived. I walked into a bar and said, in broken Spanish, “Me want work. Please, sir.” The owner told me to come back that evening, and that’s how I became a waiters’ assistant. Over the following year and a half, I took on small repair jobs, worked at a carpentry shop, and translated for a crypto exchange.
My planning horizon stretched no further than a single day. I was desperately short on money and decided things couldn’t go on that way. Maybe everyone secretly dreams of opening their own bar. I spent a long time talking the idea over with my kids. I have two sons — the younger is 8, the older 12 — and they’re up for anything: “Should we move to Argentina? Let’s do it!” “Should we open a bar? Let’s do it!”
My kids’ confidence rubbed off on me, and at the end of 2024 I borrowed $15,000 from my ex-husband to open the bar. With interest, I owed him $18,000, of which I still have $4,000 left to pay back. The money went toward paperwork, equipment, and furniture — though I dragged a lot of it in from the trash. I hauled a board off the street once and hammered together a stool out of it.
When I found a space for the bar and was on my way to sign the lease, someone stole my bag, with my passport inside, right on the street. All I had left in my pocket was a certificate showing I’d applied for residency. When the agent saw it, he tried to talk the landlord out of renting to me, pointing at the door and saying, “That door has more rights than this girl does.” But I told them my story honestly, and I talked them into it.
Opening the bar and signing contracts required a residency number I didn’t yet have, which meant a lot of bureaucratic hassle. I ran from one office to another, and somehow a solution always turned up. I managed to get everything registered with nothing more than a certificate of temporary residency.
I wasn’t issued my DNI, Argentina’s residency document, until two years after I moved. My case took a long time to review, and I had to renew my pending-asylum certificate several times.
I got really lucky with the space. The bar is upstairs, and I live in the basement with my kids. Things happen, of course — two months ago, the building’s sewer pipe clogged, sewage came pouring out of the sink, and everything flooded. It would have made a fittingly symbolic end to my story: climbing and climbing only to drown anyway. But by evening I’d found a way to fix everything and open the bar.
My kids came up with the bar’s name, Babushka. It’s less a bar than a cultural space where you can grab a drink and a bite. We have one of the largest Russian-language poetry libraries on the continent. As soon as the bar started turning a profit, I shipped four cubic meters of books over from Russia. There are books in other languages too; all sorts of things end up with me. Once, a regular customer’s mother died at the age of 100, and I inherited her library.
The bar also has homeless friends. In the evening, if there’s food left over, I feed them, and in return they bring me books they find in the trash. Some books are gifts from the authors themselves, since Argentine writers regularly perform at the bar. We hold book launches, poetry nights, film screenings, and concerts, all in Spanish.
The bar started making money almost right away. I hadn’t even finished getting all the permits, and I was already earning money hosting parties and cooking food. Even then, it was enough to get by.
For my wedding to my ex-husband, my grandmother gave me a recipe book she’d kept her whole life. I cook from it, though I sometimes improvise. I also love Asian food, so Babushka serves everything from Thai-style fried cucumbers to borscht. We make classic cocktails too, from gin and tonic to Argentina’s signature Fernet con Coca.
Only my kids and I work at the bar. I’d never actually worked at a bar before — my only prior experience was a year as a waitress in college. My older son handles the accounting spreadsheets; he’s better with finances than anyone else in the family. Friends help out too — they hang out at the bar, and when they see I’m swamped, they’ll make a sandwich or pour coffee for customers.
Two months ago, my landlord told me the rent was about to triple because my old lease was expiring. Somehow I talked him down, and the rent only doubled.
I also raise prices at the bar almost every week. That’s not my choice — everything in Argentina keeps getting more expensive, and when my supply costs go up, I have to charge customers more. Even so, by Argentine standards the bar is inexpensive — locals constantly comment that we have “nice prices.”
Over the past few years I’ve realized that stability is an illusion. This has been a time of fucking adventures. The 2000s were an anomaly — 15 fat years when everyone had great jobs and carefree travel. It’s really painful to remember that life. Back then it felt like stability had always existed, but it wasn’t so long ago that we were trying on knockoff Nikes on a piece of cardboard at the market. Now I try to appreciate the small things, like having a roof over my head and food on the table.
Mikhail Tkachevsky, 33
From a bar manager in Moscow to a photographer in New York
In college, I studied to be a paramedic and worked part-time at Il Patio. By the end of my studies, I’d realized I wanted to be a bartender instead — there was more money and more room to grow than in paramedic work. I sought out contacts in the bartending community, went to lectures, and competed in bartending competitions. In the end, I spent 12 years in the bar industry.
I worked as a bartender in Moscow at Strelka, Mendeleev Bar, and Simach, and as head manager at the bistro bar Mentalitet, where I ran the team and came up with cocktails. The war started while I was working at the bar Ess-Thetik on Patriarch’s Ponds. I immediately bought a ticket to Yerevan on the next available flight, but it was canceled, and I stayed in Russia until October — I needed to deal with a worsening anxiety disorder, save up some money, and hand off my work. Maybe it’s some Soviet instinct: the world’s on fire, but you try not to let your boss down.
After the collapse of the USSR, my parents moved to the U.S., where I was born. I don’t remember my childhood there — we came back when I was 4 — but I had an American birth certificate. I never thought much of it, since I loved Moscow and wanted to live only there; I dreamed of an apartment on Trubnaya Street. But when the mobilization started, I remembered the birth certificate. I dug around online, found out I could get an emergency passport, went to the U.S. embassy in Moscow, filed an application, and within two hours had obtained [a passport].
In November 2022, I decided to move to the U.S. I flew to New York with $5,000 I’d saved while working as a bar manager. For the first 10 days, I stayed at an expensive hostel and paid $60 a night. Then I moved to a cheaper one, sharing a three-room apartment with one shower and one toilet with 11 other people. I spent four months there, paying just $400 a month.
The whole time, I was actively job hunting. I was sure that with my experience I’d quickly land a job at a good bar, but it turned out to be very difficult. Everywhere in New York I was told that experience alone wasn’t enough — I needed experience specifically at New York bars, because everything here was “special.” Though what I remember most about that “special” treatment is going to Employees Only, one of the best bars in the U.S., and waiting 25 minutes while the bartender chatted with a friend. He finally came over and told me the only non-alcoholic drink they had was tonic water. In New York bars, it’s better to be the bartender than the customer.
My money was running out fast, so I widened my job search to other cities. I got lucky and found a job as a bar manager in Washington, convincing them I had extensive experience even though my English wasn’t perfect. The owner spoke Russian, so we were able to work things out. I moved to Washington and settled into another hostel. The work was hard because the staff had such a casual attitude toward the job — one bartender would drink heavily on shift, then not show up the next day because of a hangover, and I’d have to cover for him.
Employees showed up late, took their duties lightly, and left the workspace dirty. It was hard for me, given the OCD I’d developed behind the bar in Moscow. On top of that, the city itself struck me as boring.
After three months in Washington, I quit and went back to New York. For a couple of months I lived off the money I’d made in Washington and rented a room with my savings. I looked hard for work, but no one was hiring. Then I got lucky and landed a job at a good bar — but it was terribly dirty, which weighed on me. I felt depressed, looking for an alternative while also getting sucked into Instagram reels. My feed kept showing me beautiful reels from cinematographers and professional photographers.
I loved that kind of content, and soon I started taking photos myself on my phone. I realized I was living in the most cinematic city in the world. You walk out of your building, and there are Latin American preachers praising Christ through a crackling speaker; across the street, students are recruiting for the Communist Party; and on weekends, Ecuadorians hold volleyball tournaments. All around are supermarket carts converted into grills, with chicken wings sizzling on them.
Through Facebook, I found an American bartender who had mutual acquaintances with me from Moscow. He was just launching a bar in New York, and on the recommendation of people I knew from Moscow bars, I got hired onto the team. But the project didn’t take off — there were almost no customers. A month later, half the team was let go. I was fired too, from one day to the next with no explanation — I think because of my weak English.
I was furious and decided I no longer wanted to depend on anyone and would make my living through photography instead. I bought a camera on credit for $2,500, even though borrowing money from a bank without a credit history or steady income is pretty difficult. All I could get approved for was an Amazon credit card with terrible terms.
I lived and breathed photography: watching lectures, interviews, podcasts, trying to understand not just the technique but how good photographers think. I needed money, so I didn’t waste time — I quickly put together a portfolio from what I’d shot while learning, started posting about myself in all kinds of chats, and signed up for client-finding services. Sometimes I’d approach people on the street and say, “Want me to take your portrait?” That’s how I earned my first $40 from photography: a random passerby liked his portrait and paid me for it.
A few months after I put together my portfolio, orders started coming in through Thumbtack, a service that helps find clients for a small commission. One of my first jobs was on Long Island, shooting a business portrait, and I was paid $330 for it. Getting there and back, though, took nearly five hours. That’s when I first understood that photography isn’t just the shoot itself: it’s also endless travel, negotiations, client hunting, and knowing how to run a business.
Gradually, I developed my own style. At first I was scared to approach people and photograph them, but I quickly realized people don’t get angry when you photograph them — they smile instead. It was as if photographing them was a compliment to their looks. I started photographing people on the street at New York’s Italian culture festival.
I submitted my festival photos to a street photography contest and unexpectedly took first place, winning $1,000. What’s more, the head of the jury was none other than Bruce Gilden himself. But what made me happiest was finally being able to pay for my room. I later posted an ironic reel from the festival about photographing people without asking their permission, and it unexpectedly racked up 27 million views.
After the video blew up, I got a strange message on Instagram. The person said he really liked my style and asked me to shoot his wedding. I figured he was a scammer, since his account was empty and he’d agreed to my price without haggling. He then wrote that if things worked out, we’d fly to Las Vegas, where he’d need a photographer too.
I suggested we meet in person, and he agreed and turned out to be a real person. A few days later I shot his wedding, and then we really did fly to Las Vegas, and later to Stockholm too, for events tied to his startup, where I worked as the photographer.
Photos from his wedding were even published in Vogue, since his wife is an influencer. Since then I’ve occasionally shot events, which is how my photos also made it into Dazed. But most of my income comes from personal photo sessions. Half my clients are Russian-speaking, half English-speaking.
I haven’t gotten rich off photography. In the two years I’ve been doing this, I’ve borrowed a lot from friends and worked side jobs at catering gigs and events as a bartender. I was investing in the future more than earning money.
Only now am I starting to earn enough to cover all my expenses, and even then it’s not always enough to pay down my debts. The income is unpredictable — sometimes you land a traveling project, like the one in Stockholm, where I made $2,500 in four days; other times you won’t make that much in an entire month. Right now, to keep growing as a photographer while staying financially secure, I combine shoots with working at a cafe two days a week.
At one point I really needed money, so I worked at a bar for three months. After a shift, I had no energy left to go anywhere with my camera, so I decided it was better to earn less for now than give up photography, which brings me more joy, and I quit again.
I loved Moscow, but now I feel at home in New York. Sometimes I grab a couple of wings from an Ecuadorian food stand near my place. They call me “amigo,” and even though they barely speak English and I don’t speak Spanish, we manage to chat a little. Every time, those conversations leave me with really warm feelings — like the city has finally accepted me.
Viktoria, 42
From a farmer outside Moscow to a baker in Serbia
In the 2000s, I worked as a secretary handling document flow at a company that sold appliances. Then I moved to HR, and later I processed and issued loans at a bank. The pay was low, and the work was boring and far too monotonous.
In the early 2010s, my husband and I wanted to change something. We’d had a child with health problems, and we started thinking about moving to the countryside since our son needed clean air. We’d long wanted to start our own business so we wouldn’t depend on a boss, could plan our own days, and could earn more. So we decided to raise broiler chickens.
In 2012, we found a small house in a village in the Moscow region and left Moscow. We’d never farmed before. We figured: if it worked out, great, and if it didn’t, at least we’d have enough meat to feed ourselves.
My husband had always been building things — he worked in metalworking, assembling and fixing machines at factories — and he was excited to set up chicken production. He built a henhouse, put together a watering system, and made a brooder for the chicks. Pretty quickly we went from 50 chicks to several hundred.
Then Russia annexed Crimea. I wanted to emigrate, but my husband wasn’t ready. Life got harder — prices for feed and hatching eggs shot up several times over, and income dropped too, because people started buying less farm-raised meat.
In 2018, I finally convinced my husband that we needed to leave. We sold our equipment and moved back to Moscow to save up money for emigration. My husband got a job as an engineer at a metalworking plant, but two months later he died in a workplace accident. I spent the whole next year recovering, supporting our three children and my mother-in-law. Then COVID hit, and I was sick the whole year — emigration was the last thing on my mind.
Then the war started. My middle daughter, who was in third grade, came home from school one day and said, “It’s such a shame I can’t go to Ukraine to help our guys.” I realized my kids were being brainwashed and needed to be saved. The last straw was the growing pressure on LGBTQ+ people. My oldest child, who’s 15, is queer. Fortunately, he hasn’t run into problems because of his orientation, but I knew he wouldn’t hide his identity.
My family had already been touched by repression once before. A firing squad executed my great-grandfather in 1936. My grandfather was sent to a labor camp at 21, and my grandmother too, for “spikelets”. So I had no illusions about what could happen when the state cracks down. I couldn’t afford to delay emigrating, and nothing was keeping me in Russia anyway: my mother and husband were both dead.
Emigrating to Serbia was the simplest option. Serbia is great because, until you find a way to legalize your status, you can just do visa runs. To pay for the move, I sold my car and left in February 2023.
At first, I planned to live on the children’s survivor’s benefits. I didn’t have any specific plans for earning money — I was confident I could find some basic job.
I searched for work for several months through Telegram chats where people posted job listings, and that’s where I came across a baker position. I applied, even though I’d never worked as a baker. The bakery took a chance on me because of my farming experience and my volunteer work at a church outside Moscow, where I used to cook in the dining hall on Sundays. In June 2023, the bakery brought me on for training.
My coworkers trained me right there on the job. For three months, my training was in Serbian, even though at the time I only knew a couple of phrases. Sometimes I could guess the meaning from context. Sometimes the words resembled Russian ones. When I really didn’t understand, I used a translator.
I really loved working at the bakery, even though the pay isn’t the highest. At first I made just $500 — combined with the children’s benefits from Russia, it was enough for a modest life. But now my salary has gone up by a couple hundred dollars.
Five coworkers and I make bread and various sweet and savory pastries. The workday can run up to 10 hours, depending on how much needs to be baked. My coworkers have welcomed me, and we get along well. Overall, I like Serbia — the people are friendly, and it feels calm and safe. Plus, there’s no insane propaganda in the schools that could affect the kids.
At first, our emigration was complicated because my oldest child started having serious health problems, brought on by the change in climate and the hormonal changes of adolescence. For two years we searched for specialists and tried different treatments for him. It turned out he has high-functioning autism, and, as a result of a case of swine flu he had in 2009, narcolepsy. Compared to that, all the other “minor” problems — the lack of money, the uncertainty, being in an unfamiliar country — aren’t problems at all.
Almost all my time goes to taking care of my kids. My older son’s treatment, for example, requires frequent doctor visits and monitoring his condition. Because of that, I barely follow what’s happening in Russia. And I don’t miss it, since I don’t have any close relatives left there.
I never give up hope, though sometimes I get tired and angry. There’s no one to share the responsibility with, but I know that problems can be broken down into tasks and solved. The cost of despair is too high for me — my children’s health and lives are at stake.
Alexander Balashov, 36
From a photographer in Kemerovo to a handyman in Seattle
Before emigrating from Russia, my wife and I did wedding and commercial photography and made good money at it. The work was such that we could often sleep in until noon, though there were weeks when we only got two to three hours of sleep a night. At the same time, I worked as a brand manager, running ad campaigns and dealing with clients.
I didn’t like the situation in the country. I volunteered at Navalny’s campaign office in Kemerovo, and in 2018 I was called in for questioning in connection with the case against the office’s coordinator. A lawyer advised me to show up but invoke Article 51 of the Constitution and say nothing. A few days after the questioning, my wife and I decided to leave Russia for a while and went on a trip through Southeast Asia. We visited Thailand, Vietnam, and Cambodia.
When we came back, no one bothered me for a while. But in 2021, I started getting calls from the prosecutor’s office and the police, inviting me in for questioning without a formal summons. I refused, telling them that if they wanted to talk, they should send an official summons. But of course it was frightening. We sold our apartment in a hurry, below market price, and went into hiding.
First we went to Altai, then to Sheregesh, a small town in the Kemerovo region. I turned off my phone so I couldn’t be tracked. We then decided to leave Russia for Kyrgyzstan and plan our next steps from there. But shortly before our flight, Russia launched its war against Ukraine.
I couldn’t stay silent, so I went back to Kemerovo and staged a one-person picket with a sign reading “No to War.” I understood this was a direct path to prison, but I couldn’t act otherwise. I was detained and sentenced to 12 days. Then a cycle began: after the 12 days, I was released, but I was detained again on my way out of the holding facility for another 10 days, and then again for 13 more days. I was charged with inciting hatred “against the social group of ‘police officers’” over an old comment I’d made on [the Russian social media platform] VK, in which I harshly criticized police.
While I was in the holding facility, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Center for Combating Extremism, known as Center E, came to see me. He said I could either go to prison or cooperate, and offered to pay for my flight and expenses in Georgia in exchange for me spying on a friend who ran Navalny’s campaign office. I realized this was my chance to escape Russia and agreed. They didn’t ask me for any guarantees. I turned down the money for tickets and expenses, saying I’d rather submit receipts afterward.
Of course, I didn’t fly to Georgia. My wife and I decided we should fly straight to a country where we could stay, so we chose the United States, where we could apply for political asylum. We flew from Moscow to Qatar, then to Mexico, and from there to the U.S. border.
We took some of the money left over from selling our apartment in Kemerovo: $8,000. We decided not to take the rest so as not to draw attention at the border, fearing we wouldn’t be allowed to leave. We put some of the money into crypto and gave the rest of our savings to friends, family, and animal shelters.
We showed up at the U.S. border six times, and each time we were turned back. You can only request asylum right at the border or after you’ve crossed it. But American border agents stand before the border itself, thoroughly checking documents and vehicles, and if they suspect you might be an asylum seeker, they send you back. Our seventh attempt succeeded because the cars in the lane we were driving in weren’t being checked.
We applied for asylum, and after that, my wife and I were sent to separate immigration detention facilities, since asylum applications are always reviewed individually.
I was in immigration detention for almost four months. I spent a lot of time in the facility’s law library, where I learned about immigration law and found phone numbers for law firms. I called around and that’s how I found a free lawyer.
One of the conditions for getting out of immigration detention is having a sponsor in the U.S. — someone who will vouch for you and provide housing and food. I got lucky and found a sponsor while still detained: a guy in the facility with me had a friend who’d moved to the U.S. from Ukraine long ago, and that friend became a sponsor for both me and my “cellmate.”
After getting out of detention, I still had to get my wife out. While I was detained, I’d had almost no contact with her. I looked into it and learned she’d only be released on bail of $35,000. I didn’t have that kind of money.
I was preparing for the hearing that would decide whether my asylum petition would be approved, while also looking for money to get my wife released. My sponsor let me stay with him and offered me work with him on a construction site. I agreed and searched for other work at the same time — checking job listings online, asking people around me, and reaching out to friends of friends.
I soon found work on a skyscraper construction site, even though I’d never done anything like that in Russia. With money from that job, I moved out from my sponsor’s place and rented a room. But there was no way to quickly earn the $35,000 for my wife’s bail through construction work. So I turned to a company that specializes in exactly these situations — it pays your bail for you, and you pay it back later with a fee on top.
My wife was eventually released, after spending six months in detention. I kept working on the skyscraper construction site in Washington, while she got a job as a cleaner, cleaning apartments for pay. We had almost no free time — I’d sometimes wake up at three in the morning, work all day, and go to bed at ten at night. My wife was exhausted too. We lived like that for several months.
In early 2023, the skyscraper was finished, and I started looking for other ways to make money. In Russia, I’d never worked with my hands — I’d only done things around my own house. But I do have an engineering degree, so figuring out repair work wasn’t hard for me.
On Facebook, I found a Russian-speaking woman who’d moved to the U.S. with her parents as a child. She bought old RVs, fixed them up, and sold them. I got a job with her doing repairs and made about $25 an hour. That went on for several months, and then she moved on to other pursuits, leaving me without work.
I started looking for jobs on sites offering small repair services. I replaced toilets, installed doors, and painted rooms. Life in the U.S. is very expensive, so I had to grab anything that brought in income and work without days off.
My wife and I got lucky — in December 2024, we won our case and received a document allowing us to stay in the U.S. We wanted to get back into photography, which meant buying equipment and investing in marketing. But our marriage gradually started falling apart. My wife and I had built up mutual resentment, partly because of the drastic lifestyle change and the enormous stress. We tried to save the relationship, but it was hard to hear each other out. Little by little we stopped talking, even though we kept living together. I was the one who initiated the divorce. Attempts to reconnect didn’t work, and we didn’t have the energy to keep trying. Technically, though, we’re not divorced yet — we’re still working through the paperwork.
Soon after we split up, I moved to Seattle, focused on repair work, and became a “jack of all trades,” or handyman, as it’s called here. In the U.S. there are several platforms where you can hire workers like that.
Some jobs are simple: changing a lock or a faucet. But sometimes there are trickier ones, like framing a house. The work varies widely: laying tile, installing a bathtub, replacing a toilet, fixing a gate. Sometimes the job isn’t building something but tearing it down — a wall, say.
I realized that working with your hands is great. On top of that, it’s quite profitable for people without local degrees or certifications. I make between $8,000 and $12,000 a month, depending on how much work I take on. Usually I have up to six small jobs a day, but sometimes there’s one big job that takes a whole day or even several days.
I prepare for jobs in advance. For example, I knew nothing about installing automatic garage doors, but I researched it all online, showed up, and did it as if I’d been doing it my whole life. There’s tons of information online now about how to do repairs — there’s a YouTube video for almost any problem, or you can ask an AI. Prep usually takes a little time, anywhere from half an hour to an hour. Sometimes I just figure it out myself, working out logically how something is put together.
A typical summer workday runs 10–12 hours, so I make my own food and bring it with me. Travel eats up some of my time too — I might spend an hour getting from one job to the next.
Sometimes I work without days off — it’s easier for me to put in a lot of hours all at once so I’ll have more time later to relax somewhere beautiful. Ideally, I’d like to work a couple of weeks a month, or every other month, and spend the rest of my time traveling.
I feel like I belong in the U.S. now. Americans, in general, are a lot like Russians — just more successful and kinder. I don’t miss Russia much, since most of my friends have scattered elsewhere. They live all over the world: in England, Australia, the European Union. Some live in the U.S. too — by coincidence, some old friends of mine from Kemerovo now live in the town next to mine. But I keep close track of what’s happening in Russia and get into arguments about it on social media.
I love my work and consider myself a very happy person. Though I do hope that my ex-wife and I will get back into photography together — if not as a married couple, then as business partners.
